title: Margery Kempe
hookLine: a loud, weeping English pilgrim who dictated her life to a scribe, and wouldn't stop crying in church

lines: SHE TELLS HER LIFE TO A SCRIBE.
cards: A sermon is under way in an English church, and a woman in white is sobbing. Not quietly: loudly enough that the preacher stops. Some of the congregation glare.
Some mutter that she's faking, or sick, or showing off. One friar, her own book says, refuses to preach while she's in the building.

She's a married woman from the town of Lynn, a mother, a former businesswoman whose brewery failed. She can't read or write. And she has decided to tell her whole life anyway, out loud, to a scribe who will write it down.

teach.b: The Book of Margery Kempe is her story in her own telling, though she never calls herself I. She calls herself this creature. This creature went to Jerusalem.
This creature was rebuked. It isn't a polished book. It's restless, funny in places, and honest about how much she annoyed people.

teach.h: CRYING AT THE PLACE OF THE CROSS.
teach.b: On pilgrimage in Jerusalem, the Book says, standing where Jesus was crucified, she fell down and cried out as if her heart would burst, and the crying came back again and again for years: when she thought of the Passion, when she saw a baby boy, when she saw a man being beaten.
Fellow pilgrims got so tired of her that they left her behind. Clergy questioned her. More than once she was accused of heresy, and more than once she talked her way out of it.
So was it holiness, or something else? Her neighbors argued about that, and readers still do. The Book doesn't settle it.
But it records a visit she made to Julian, the anchoress at Norwich.

teach.h: JULIAN SAYS: TEARS CAN BE A GIFT.
teach.b: Margery poured out her fears, and Julian, the Book says, told her that the Holy Spirit never moves a soul against love, and that a soul's tears can be a sign of the Spirit at work.
Then, the Book adds, the two women talked together for days. The Gospels show Jesus weeping too. The King James Bible gives it in two words: "Jesus wept."
Margery's neighbors found her tears too much. She kept weeping, and kept going.

how: Christians today read The Book of Margery Kempe as a window into late medieval devotion, and some find in it permission for loud, emotional prayer; the Church of England remembers her in its calendar.

games.q: you're Margery, in church. the sermon touches you and the tears start coming, loud. people are turning around. what do you do?
o: slip out quietly before anyone notices.
try to swallow it, and fail.
decide never to go to church again.
games.why: the Book says she tried to hold the crying back, and it came anyway. she kept going to church, and on pilgrimage, tears and all.

practice: Notice what's in you right now, without trimming it down: if it's sadness, let it be the size it is; if it's gladness, the same; if nothing much is there, that's fine too.
Think of one thing you usually hold back, a laugh, a thank-you said with feeling, a song in the car. If you pray, bring whatever is there to God as it is, not tidied first.

wordCard.voice: Margery Kempe. An English wife, mother and pilgrim who wept loudly at prayer, told her life to a scribe, and called herself this creature.

carryVoice: Your line: tears are allowed. What moves you can come to prayer untidied. See you tomorrow.
